classification.instruction: Classify each family BEFORE creating anything. A TypeORM entity existing in source is NOT evidence that its table should exist.

Creating `report` and `finding` would re-establish the mutable report model that the immutable inspection report deliberately replaced, producing a second divergent source of report truth.

sc4.defect: user.subscriptionStatus database DEFAULT 'active' against an entity declaring 'none'. An INSERT omitting the column produced an account asserting an ACTIVE subscription — the value the entitlement layer reads as a paying customer.
sc4.repair: migration 1800000026000-UserSubscriptionStatusDefault: ALTER TABLE "user" ALTER COLUMN "subscriptionStatus" SET DEFAULT 'none'. The entity was already correct; the database was wrong.
sc4.deliberatelyNotDone: No existing row read or rewritten. Existing 'active' rows are legitimate customer subscription state and a migration cannot distinguish those from rows that inherited the bad default.
sc4.measuredRestraint: A fresh production backup restored and upgraded in a disposable database: the distribution of existing subscriptionStatus values is byte-identical across the migration (9 active / 57 none, before and after).
preserved: EN-3: registration still produces free/none and capability still comes from a bounded grant
BI-4: a caller-supplied subscriptionStatus is still refused 400

productionUpgradeRehearsal.structuralConvergence: 0 material differences between the upgraded restored-production schema and the committed canonical manifest
productionUpgradeRehearsal.residualDigestDifferenceAccountedFor: Production carries 9 tables a fresh replay deliberately does not build (control_verifications, finding, hazard_taxonomy, outcomes, regulatory_profile, report, report_attachments, standards, users) plus the user.password / user.legacy_id columns §305 preserved without replicating.

sc3TablesInProduction.significance: All four are synchronize-era residue and ALL ARE EMPTY. Retirement loses no customer data. §305 forbids dropping production-only tables, so they remain in place and are now inert.

productionUpgradeRehearsal.severityCorrection: On a migration-built database the affected routes returned 500. In today's production the tables happen to exist, so they would have returned an empty result. SC-3 is a REBUILT-ENVIRONMENT failure — disaster recovery, any new environment, and every disposable verification database take the replay path — not a live 500 a beta customer was hitting.

gateHonesty.risk: §310 resolved SC-3 by REMOVING entities, so the entity-contract gate stops comparing them. A shrinking entity set could make a gate green with nothing repaired.
controls: §309's F-1 was rewritten from 'these four entities fail to read' into the GENERAL property — no entity in the DataSource maps to a table absent from the database — asserted over all 57 registered entities, so it cannot go green by looking at fewer.
F-1 was WATCHED TO FAIL: a probe entity mapped to a non-existent table was registered, F-1 failed, and the probe was removed (tsc clean, no git residue).
The four retired entities are ENUMERATED in entity-contract.baseline.json under sc3ClosedAt310 rather than merely deleted.
SC-3's closure rests on the ROUTE PROOF driving live routes against a real database, not on a gate going quiet.
The canonical schema gate is unaffected by entity removal: it compares a replayed database against the manifest and would still fail if a described table went missing. Table count is unchanged at 68.

toolingKept.scripts/print-deployed-routes.ts: npm run routes:deployed:db — the authoritative deployed route table. Kept because reading controllers gave the WRONG answer and this gave the right one; it also makes route-surface change reviewable by diff.

knownResidue.why: These import modules §310 deleted. They are NOT compiled (tsconfig includes only src/**/*), are referenced by no npm script, and back no deployed route. They were left in place DELIBERATELY: their paths are digested members of frozen manifests (verification/expert-hazlenz-checkpoint-consolidation-2026-09-07/POST-CONSOLIDATION-MANIFEST.sha256) and of verification/current/MUTATING-SCRIPTS.json, so deleting them would be a manifest fault. Recorded here rather than silently swept.
